parakeet: A person can sincerely believe they're loving you while teaching you to hate yourself. A parent can sincerely believe they're protecting their child while teaching that child to fear their own body. A pastor can sincerely believe they're guarding the flock while training people to distrust outsiders. A community can sincerely believe it's preserving the truth while punishing honest questions. That's the tragedy. The harm doesn't always require evil intentions. Sometimes all it requires is a simple moral story, a scared community, a trusted authority, and a belief system that tells people their certainty came from somewhere higher than themselves. That's why religion is not the whole disease. It's a delivery system. It delivers certainty, it delivers belonging, identity, moral categories, it delivers rituals, language, leaders, and stories that make the world feel easier to understand. And for people living in fear, grief, loneliness, trauma, or instability, that can feel deeply comforting. But comfort is not the same as truth. Belonging is not the same as freedom, and certainty is not the same as wisdom. So if we want to understand religious harm clearly, we have to go deeper than religion bad. Because religion bad may be emotionally satisfying, but it's not enough. The more important question is what is it about us that made religion work so well? Was what is it about us that made inherited certainty so appealing? What is it about us that made sacred authority so persuasive? What is it about us that made simple answers feel safer than honest questions?
